## Proof

**Claim:** Yes, such subsets exist.

**Key identity.** For every positive integer $n$,
$$\sum_{d \mid n} \varphi(d) = n,$$
where $\varphi$ is Euler's totient function. Consequently, for any $i, j$,
$$\gcd(i,j) = \sum_{d \mid \gcd(i,j)} \varphi(d) = \sum_{\substack{d \mid i \\ d \mid j}} \varphi(d). \tag{1}$$

**Construction.** Since $\mathbb{N}$ is infinite, we can choose pairwise disjoint finite subsets $S_d \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ (one for each $d \geq 1$) with $|S_d| = \varphi(d)$. (For example, enumerate $d = 1, 2, 3, \dots$ and assign to each $S_d$ a fresh block of $\varphi(d)$ previously unused natural numbers; this is possible since we are placing countably many finite sets into an infinite set.)

Now define, for each $i \geq 1$,
$$A_i \;=\; \bigcup_{d \mid i} S_d. \tag{2}$$

**Verification of $|A_i| = i$.** Since the $S_d$ are pairwise disjoint,
$$|A_i| = \sum_{d \mid i} |S_d| = \sum_{d \mid i} \varphi(d) = i. \tag{3}$$
In particular $|A_i \cap A_i| = |A_i| = i = \gcd(i,i)$. ✓

**Verification of $|A_i \cap A_j| = \gcd(i,j)$ for $i \neq j$.** Using pairwise disjointness of the $S_d$ again,
$$A_i \cap A_j = \Big(\bigcup_{d \mid i} S_d\Big) \cap \Big(\bigcup_{e \mid j} S_e\Big) = \bigcup_{\substack{d \mid i \\ d \mid j}} S_d = \bigcup_{d \mid \gcd(i,j)} S_d.$$
Therefore
$$|A_i \cap A_j| = \sum_{d \mid \gcd(i,j)} |S_d| = \sum_{d \mid \gcd(i,j)} \varphi(d) = \gcd(i,j), \tag{4}$$
where the last step uses identity (1).

**Consistency check on the common element.** Since $1 \mid i$ for every $i$, every $A_i$ contains $S_1$, and $|S_1| = \varphi(1) = 1$. Thus all the $A_i$ share exactly the single element of $S_1$, matching $|A_1 \cap A_j| = \gcd(1,j) = 1$ for all $j$. ✓

All conditions are satisfied, so the desired family $\{A_i\}_{i \geq 1}$ exists. $\blacksquare$
